problem:
For what reason does the function $f(x)$ given below have a discontinuity at $x=-1?$

$$
f(x)={\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}+1}{2}, & x<-1 \\ 2, & x=-1 \\ \frac{2}{{x}^{2}+1}, & x>-1\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.problem:
For what reason does the function $f(x)$ given below have a discontinuity at $x=-2?$

$$
f(x)={\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}+4}{2}, & x<-2 \\ 4, & x=-2 \\ \frac{2}{{x}^{2}+4}, & x>-2\end{aligned}
$$
feedback.worked_solution:
Let's check the conditions necessary for $f(x)$ to be continuous at $x=-2.$

- $f(-2)=4,$ so $f(-2)$ exists. $✓$

- We calculate the one-sided limits and check if they coincide:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (-2)^{-}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to (-2)^{-}}(\frac{{x}^{2}+4}{2}) \\  & =\frac{(-2)^{2}+4}{2} \\  & =\frac{4+4}{2} \\  & =4, \\ {lim}_{x\to (-2)^{+}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to (-2)^{+}}(\frac{2}{{x}^{2}+4}) \\  & =\frac{2}{(-2)^{2}+4} \\  & =\frac{2}{4+4} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the one-sided limits exist but are not equal. $\times $

Therefore, the function $f(x)$ has a discontinuity at $x=-2$ because ${lim}_{x\to (-2)}f(x)$ does not exist.
